Milnor · Morse Theory · the shortest path

Morse Theory, the shortest path

The main theorems of Milnor’s Morse Theory, and exactly what their formal proofs use: a route through the book read off the dependency graph of its Lean formalization.

98,053 lines of Lean825 trace tags810 declarations citedLean 4.33.1 · Mathlib · October 2026

A trace tag looks like this: Chapter2/CellAttachSubmanifoldtheorem_3_2_attach_submanifold, a file of the project and the declaration in it that proves the sentence; every tag in this text names a declaration on the path. Each chapter opens on its own; use the contents or the links at the end of a chapter.

0. The path

This text proves the main theorems of Milnor’s Morse Theory and nothing else. Which results count as needed is not a matter of taste: it is read off the Lean formalization of the book, by following the formal proofs of the main theorems back through every declaration they use. What they use is proved or stated here, in the order of the dependencies; what they do not use is left out, and Appendix B lists it.

This is the third part of the project. The first, Morse Theory, Rewritten, is the whole book with all the details and some applications, for advanced undergraduates. The second, Morse Theory, Checked, is the Lean formalization with its faithfulness checks: the verified edition, the proof by proof, the comparison of each result with its formal statement, and the round-trip audit. This part keeps only what the main theorems need.

0.1 The main theorems

The path ends at the twelve main theorems below, each proved in the chapter shown. The last columns give what each one needs: the number of declarations of the formalization its proof uses (“Decls.”), the number of results of the verified edition among them, and the chapters of this text it rests on.

Four of them are used by no other main theorem: Theorem 3.5, the existence of Morse functions, the Morse inequalities and the fundamental theorem 17.3. The rest form a chain. The lemma of Morse and Theorems 3.1 and 3.2, the index theorem, Theorem 17.1 and Theorem 22.1 lead to the two periodicity theorems, which stand side by side: the orthogonal case uses the material of the unitary chapter, but not its theorem.

0.2 How the path was found

A formal proof is a graph. Every declaration of the formalization, definition or theorem, refers in its statement and in its proof to other declarations, and Lean records these references exactly. The script Exposition/shortest/DepDump.lean writes the graph out: one node for each declaration of this project and of the companion project (the formalization of Milnor’s Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint, on which this one is built), and an edge for every direct use. Declarations of Mathlib are leaves, since Mathlib cannot depend on either project. Exposition/shortest/deps.py then starts from the formal statements of the main theorems and follows the edges back. The declarations it reaches are the path.

Of the 6,287 declarations of this project, 3,888 are on the path (62%); of the 1,799 of the companion project, 147 are. Of the results of the verified edition, 239 are on the path and 158 are not.

Each result of the verified edition (Exposition/Verification.md) names the declarations that prove it, and a result is on the path when one of them is. These results are the units of this text: every one of them appears, labelled by its number in the verified edition (Milnor’s Theorem 3.2, for instance, is result V2.8), and no other result does. Every trace tag in the text, such as Chapter2/CellAttachSubmanifoldtheorem_3_2_attach_submanifold, names a declaration that the script found on the path; Exposition/shortest/check.py verifies this for every tag. Appendix A gives, for each result, the results it uses directly.

Two cautions. The path is the one these proofs take. A different proof could need less, and a result off the path can still be worth knowing. It is also the path in the setting the formalization chose. Manifolds are submanifolds of a Euclidean space and “complete” becomes “closed in the Euclidean space”; homology has coefficients in a field; cell complexes are iterated adjunction spaces; and the limits of §§23–24 are replaced by finite stages. Every Riemannian manifold is such a submanifold, by the theorems of Whitney and Nash, but those theorems are not on the path.

0.3 What the graph shows

Some of what the dependencies say is not visible in the book’s order of presentation.

  • Part I and the rest meet only at the start. Theorem 3.5, the existence of Morse functions and the Morse inequalities are used by no later main theorem. The homology of Chapter 4 is used by nothing after it, because the fundamental theorem and Bott periodicity are statements about homotopy types and homotopy groups. Still, Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 are used throughout, and Sard’s theorem and the generic perturbations behind Corollary 6.8 come back in the proof of Theorem 22.1.
  • The fundamental theorem does not need the index theorem. Theorem 17.3 needs only that the index of the energy at a geodesic equals the index of its restriction to broken geodesics (Theorem 16.2). The index theorem is needed to compute indices, and only Bott periodicity does that.
  • Bott periodicity does not need the fundamental theorem. It needs Theorem 17.1 (piecewise smooth paths suffice), through Corollary 22.2, and Theorem 22.1, but not Theorem 17.3.
  • Much of the geometry is never used. Parallel transport, sectional curvature, the curvature of a totally geodesic submanifold, the Hopf–Rinow theorem in full (only the existence of a shortest geodesic is used, for the distance from \(I\) to \(-I\)), Theorem 18.1 and the density of non-conjugate points are all off the path. The fundamental theorem simply assumes its end points non-conjugate.
  • The algebra of §§21, 23 and 24 is replaced. The Lie-algebra computations of §21, Milnor’s eigenvectors of \(K_A\) in §23 and the spectral counts of §24 are off the path. Indices are computed from Jacobi fields (explicit ones for \(SU(n)\), Killing fields for the spaces \(\Omega_k(n)\)) and the index theorem.

0.4 What is assumed

The path rests on Mathlib and on the companion project, and on nothing else. From the companion project it uses fifty theorems directly. In substance they are:

  • the inverse function theorem on manifolds Milnor/Chapter1/InverseFunctionisLocalDiffeomorphAt_of_isInvertible_mfderiv;
  • slice submanifolds and their charts Milnor/Chapter2/SubmanifoldIsSliceSubmanifold, with regular level sets as slice submanifolds Milnor/Chapter2/LevelSetisSliceSubmanifold_preimage;
  • Sard’s theorem Milnor/Chapter3/Sardsard;
  • the \(\varepsilon\)-neighbourhood (tubular) construction Milnor/Chapter6/Tubular1Tub.injective_fderiv_φ and the normal bundle as a slice submanifold Milnor/Chapter8/NormalBundleProblems.isSliceSubmanifold_normalBundle;
  • smooth approximation on compact sets Milnor/Chapter8/ApproxProblems.exists_contDiff_approx_of_isCompact.

From Mathlib it uses about 3,900 theorems directly. The substantial ones fall under a few headings:

  • Calculus: derivatives, the mean value theorem, Taylor’s formula, the inverse function theorem.
  • Ordinary differential equations: Picard–Lindelöf Mathlib/Analysis/ODE/PicardLindelofIsPicardLindelof and Grönwall’s inequality.
  • Linear algebra: Sylvester’s law of inertia Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/QuadraticForm/SignaturesigNeg_isGreatest, the spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices Mathlib/Analysis/Matrix/SpectrumMatrix.IsHermitian.spectral_theorem, the continuous functional calculus, the matrix exponential, determinants, Gram–Schmidt, quaternions and Clifford algebras.
  • Measure theory: Lebesgue and Haar measure, and null sets.
  • Topology: compactness, the Lebesgue number lemma, bump functions, paths and homotopies, homotopy groups as Mathlib defines them, and covering maps (for the circle).
  • Homological algebra: chain complexes, their homology, the long exact sequence of a short exact sequence of complexes, and the singular chain complex.

Everything else is proved in Chapters 1–10. The infrastructure that the formalization had to build because Mathlib does not have it is marked “Fact (standard)”: relative singular homology and excision, homotopy lifting and the exact homotopy sequence of a fibration, mapping telescopes, and smooth dependence on initial conditions. It is stated precisely, with an indication of the proof; the formal proofs are in the files the tags name.

0.5 How to read

Results are labelled by their number in the verified edition, and a reference to another result gives that number and the section where the result is proved: “[V1.8, §1.6]”. To reach one theorem, read the chapters listed for it in §0.1. Within a chapter the order is a dependency order, so nothing is used before it is stated.

1. Critical points and the lemma of Morse →

1. Critical points and the lemma of Morse

This chapter fixes the setting and the vocabulary (critical points, the Hessian, index, nullity) and proves the lemma of Morse on a manifold and the isolation of non-degenerate critical points; every main theorem rests on it. A manifold \(M\) is here Mathlib’s: smooth, without boundary, modelled on a real normed space \(E\), with no Hausdorff or countability hypothesis. The torus of §1, the examples of degenerate critical points, the converse of the lemma of Morse and Lemma 2.4 are not needed; the flows behind Lemma 2.4 are stated where Theorem 3.1 uses them [V1.14, §2.2].

1.1 The setting

  • \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real inner product space. A manifold is a slice submanifold \(N \subseteq V\) modelled on \(Z\), \(n = \dim Z\), not necessarily closed, with tangent spaces \(T_qN \subseteq V\) and projections \(P_q\) (§1.4).
  • A function on \(N\) is a restriction \(f = F|N = F \circ \iota\) of a smooth \(F : V \to \mathbb R\), \(\iota\) the inclusion; its critical points, Hessian, index and nullity are those of §1.2, computed in any chart.
  • The metric is induced by \(V\); “complete” becomes “closed in \(V\)”, which makes closed Riemannian balls compact.
  • Cell complexes are iterated adjunction spaces, finitely or countably many cells attached one at a time along arbitrary maps [V2.11, §2.7].
  • Homology is singular, with coefficients in a field \(\mathbb k\). Homotopy groups are Mathlib’s \(\pi_i(X, x)\); “\(\cong\)” between them means a bijection (not claimed to respect base points) unless “as groups” is said.
  • Paths are maps \(\mathbb R \to V\) used on \([0, 1]\); \(\Omega(N; p, q)\) is the space of piecewise smooth paths in \(N\) from \(p\) to \(q\) with Milnor’s pseudometric; \(E\), \(E_{**}\) and \(\Omega^d\) are the energy, its Hessian at a geodesic and the paths of least energy \(d\).

Definition (attaching a cell) [V1.2]. Let \(D^n\), \(S^{n-1}\) be the closed unit ball and sphere of \(\mathbb R^n\) (\(S^{-1} = \emptyset\)). For a continuous \(\varphi : S^{n-1} \to X\), \(X \cup_\varphi e^n\) is the pushout of \(\varphi\) and \(S^{n-1} \hookrightarrow D^n\): the quotient of \(X \sqcup D^n\) by \(u \sim \varphi(u)\). A map out of it is a pair of maps on \(X\) and on \(D^n\) agreeing along \(\varphi\). Chapter2/AttachingAttachCell Chapter2/AttachingcellDesc

1.2 Critical points, the Hessian, the index

Definition [V5.1, V1.3]. Let \(f : E \to \mathbb R\). A point \(p\) is critical if \(f\) has derivative \(0\) at \(p\). The Hessian \(d^2f_p(v, w) = D(x \mapsto df_x w)(p)\,v\) is the second derivative, defined everywhere and symmetric where \(f\) is \(C^2\). A continuous bilinear form \(H\) has null space \(\{v : H(v, \cdot) = 0\}\) and nullity its dimension; it is non-degenerate if the null space is \(0\); its index is Mathlib’s negative index of inertia of \(v \mapsto H(v, v)\). For finite-dimensional \(E\) the index is the largest dimension of a subspace on which \(H(v, v) < 0\) for \(v \ne 0\), and non-degenerate means nullity \(0\). Chapter1/NondegenerateIsCriticalPoint Chapter1/Nondegeneratehessian Chapter1/Nondegenerateindex_isGreatest

Definition [V1.4]. Let \(f : M \to \mathbb R\) and \(\kappa_p\) the preferred chart at \(p\). The point \(p\) is critical if \(df_p = 0\). The Hessian \(f_{**}\) is \(d^2(f \circ \kappa_p^{-1})\) at \(\kappa_p(p)\), a form on \(T_pM = E\); the index and nullity of \(f\) at \(p\) are those of \(f_{**}\); \(p\) is a non-degenerate critical point if it is critical and \(f_{**}\) is non-degenerate. A Morse function is a smooth function whose critical points are all non-degenerate. Chapter1/ManifoldIsCriticalPointM Chapter1/ManifoldhessianM Chapter1/ManifoldIsMorseFunction

1.3 Independence of the coordinates

Theorem [V1.5]. (i) If \(\psi\) is \(C^2\) at \(q\) and \(f\) is \(C^2\) at \(\psi(q)\), then \[d^2(f \circ \psi)_q(v, w) = d^2f_{\psi(q)}(d\psi_q v, d\psi_q w) + df_{\psi(q)}(d^2\psi_q(v, w)),\] and the last term vanishes if \(df_{\psi(q)} = 0\). Chapter1/Manifoldhessian_comp_apply Chapter1/Nondegeneratehessian_comp (ii) A smooth coordinate system is an open partial homeomorphism \(y\) from \(M\) to a normed space, smooth on its domain, with inverse smooth on its image (with values in \(E\): a chart of the maximal atlas). Let \(p \in \operatorname{dom} y\). If \(f\) is differentiable at \(p\), then \(p\) is critical iff \(y(p)\) is critical for \(f \circ y^{-1}\). If \(f\) is \(C^2\) at the critical point \(p\), then \(d^2(f \circ y^{-1})_{y(p)}\) has the non-degeneracy, index and nullity of \(f_{**}\). Chapter1/ManifoldIsSmoothCoord Chapter1/ManifoldIsSmoothCoord.isCriticalPointM_iff Chapter1/ManifoldIsSmoothCoord.index_eq Chapter1/ManifoldIsSmoothCoord.nullity_eq

Proof. (i) Near \(q\), \(d(f \circ \psi)_x = df_{\psi(x)} \circ d\psi_x\); differentiate at \(q\) by the product rule. (ii) The transition \(\tau = \kappa_p \circ y^{-1}\) is smooth near \(y(p)\) with invertible derivative \(L\), and \(f \circ y^{-1} = (f \circ \kappa_p^{-1}) \circ \tau\) there. The chain rule handles criticality; at a critical point (i) gives \(d^2(f \circ y^{-1})_{y(p)} = f_{**}(L\,\cdot, L\,\cdot)\). A pull-back by an isomorphism has the same index (Mathlib’s index is invariant under isometries) and nullity Chapter1/Nondegenerateindex_bilinearComp. \(\square\)

1.4 Functions on a slice submanifold

A slice chart for \(N \subseteq V\) is a diffeomorphism \(\sigma\) of an open subset of \(V\) onto one of \(Z \times W\) such that a point of its domain lies in \(N\) iff the \(W\)-component of its image is \(0\). \(N\) is a slice submanifold if slice charts cover it Milnor/Chapter2/SubmanifoldIsSliceSubmanifold; it is a manifold modelled on \(Z\) with charts \(q \mapsto \sigma(q)_Z\), inverted by the parametrizations \(x(z) = \sigma^{-1}(z, 0)\) Chapter1/ManifoldSubmanifoldsliceParam.

Definition [V6.1]. \(T_qN\) is the range of \(d\iota_q\) and \(P_q\) the orthogonal projection of \(V\) onto it (smooth in \(q\) [V6.2, §5.1]). For \(g : N \to E'\), \(d^Ng_q = dg_q \circ \tau_q : V \to E'\), where \(\tau_q(v) = (d\sigma_q v)_Z\) for the slice chart \(\sigma\) chosen at \(q\); only its values on \(T_qN\), written \(dg_q\), are used. If \(g = G\) on \(N\) near \(q\) for a \(G : V \to E'\) differentiable at \(q\), then \(dg_q = dG_q\) on \(T_qN\). Chapter1/ManifoldSubmanifoldtangentSubspace Chapter6/ProjectiontanProj Chapter6/ProjectiondN Chapter6/ProjectiondN_eq_fderiv

Proof. \(\tau_q \circ d\iota_q\) is the derivative of the chart at \(q\) read in itself, the identity, so \(d\iota_q(\tau_q v) = v\) on \(T_qN\); apply the chain rule to \(G \circ \iota\). \(\square\)

Theorem [V1.6]. Let \(q \in N\) lie in the domain of a slice chart \(\sigma\) with parametrization \(x\), \(u = \sigma(q)_Z\), and \(F : V \to \mathbb R\).

  1. \(T_qN\) is the range of \(dx_u\).
  2. If \(F\) is differentiable at \(q\): \(q\) is critical for \(F|N\) iff \(u\) is critical for \(F \circ x\), iff \(dF_q\) vanishes on \(T_qN\).
  3. If \(F\) is \(C^2\) at \(q\) and \(q\) is critical for \(F|N\), the index and nullity of \(F|N\) at \(q\) are those of \(d^2(F \circ x)_u\).
  4. For \(L_p(y) = \|y - p\|^2\): \(q\) is critical for \(L_p|N\) iff \(q - p \perp T_qN\); if \(x\) is \(C^2\) at \(u\), \(d^2(L_p \circ x)_u(v, w) = 2\big(\langle dx_u v, dx_u w\rangle + \langle d^2x_u(v, w), x(u) - p\rangle\big)\); at a critical \(q\) the nullity of \(L_p|N\) is that of this form.

Chapter1/ManifoldSubmanifoldtangentSubspace_eq_range_fderiv_sliceParam Chapter1/ManifoldSubmanifoldisCriticalPointM_comp_val_iff_forall_tangent Chapter1/ManifoldSubmanifoldindex_hessian_comp_sliceParam Chapter1/ManifoldSubmanifoldnullityM_normSq_sub_eq

Proof. The chart induced by \(\sigma\) is in the maximal atlas, and \(F|N\) read in it is \(F \circ x\) near \(u\): §1.3 gives the first part of 2, and 3. Near \(q\), \(\iota = x \circ (\text{chart})\) with the chart’s derivative invertible: this is 1. The chain rule \(d(F|N)_q = dF_q \circ d\iota_q\) gives the rest of 2. For 4, \(dL_p(y) = 2\langle y - p, \cdot\rangle\), \(d^2L_p = 2\langle\cdot, \cdot\rangle\), and §1.3 (i) applies with its first-order term, Milnor’s second-fundamental-form term (p. 36) Chapter1/ManifoldSubmanifoldhessian_normSq_sub_comp. \(\square\)

1.5 Hadamard’s lemma

Lemma 2.1, to second order [V1.7]. Let \(O \subseteq E\) be open and star-shaped about \(0\), and \(f\) smooth on \(O\) with values in a complete space, \(f(0) = 0\), \(df_0 = 0\). Then \(f(x) = B(x)(x, x)\) on \(O\), where \(B(x) = \int_0^1 (1 - t)\, d^2f_{tx}\, dt\) is smooth on \(O\) and symmetric, and \(B(0) = \tfrac12 d^2f_0\). Chapter1/Hadamardexists_hadamard_two_on

Proof. Taylor’s formula with integral remainder along \([0, x] \subseteq O\). Smoothness of \(B\) is differentiation under the integral sign, which Milnor does not argue: if \(h\) is \(C^n\) on an open \(U \subseteq E \times \mathbb R\) containing \(O \times [0, 1]\), then \(x \mapsto \int_0^1 h(x, t)\, dt\) is \(C^n\) on \(O\) Chapter1/HadamardcontDiffOn_intervalIntegral, by induction on \(n\), dominating the integrand on a tube around \(\{x_0\} \times [0, 1]\). \(\square\)

1.6 The lemma of Morse

Lemma 2.2 (the lemma of Morse) [V1.8]. Let \(E\) be finite-dimensional, \(n = \dim E\), \(f\) smooth on an open \(U \ni p\), and \(p\) critical with \(d^2f_p\) non-degenerate of index \(\lambda\). There is an open partial homeomorphism \(y : E \to \mathbb R^n\), smooth with smooth inverse, \(p \in \operatorname{dom} y \subseteq U\), \(y(p) = 0\), with \[f = f(p) - \textstyle\sum_{i < \lambda} y_i^2 + \sum_{i \ge \lambda} y_i^2 \quad \text{on } \operatorname{dom} y.\] The same holds on \(M\), for \(p\) a non-degenerate critical point of index \(\lambda\), with \(y\) a smooth coordinate system. Chapter1/MorseLemmamorse_lemma Chapter1/ManifoldMorsemorse_lemmaM

Proof. Not Milnor’s induction, which needs an unjustified linear change making \(H_{rr}(0) \ne 0\), but one application of the inverse function theorem. First a chart \(\varphi\), smooth with smooth inverse, \(\varphi(p) = 0\), \(d\varphi_p = \mathrm{id}\), \(f = f(p) + \tfrac12 d^2f_p(\varphi, \varphi)\) Chapter1/MorseLemmaexists_morse_chart.

  1. On a ball \(O\) with \(p + O \subseteq U\), \(f(p + x) - f(p) = B(x)(x, x)\) by §1.5, and \(B_0 = B(0) = \tfrac12 d^2f_p\) is symmetric and non-degenerate.
  2. On linear maps of \(E\) let \(\Psi(T) = B_0(T\cdot, T\cdot) + B_0(T\cdot, \cdot) - B_0(\cdot, T\cdot)\). Then \(\Psi(\mathrm{id}) = B_0\), \(\Psi(T)(v, v) = B_0(Tv, Tv)\) by symmetry, and \(d\Psi_{\mathrm{id}}(K) = 2B_0(K\cdot, \cdot)\) is invertible, as \(v \mapsto B_0(v, \cdot)\) is an injective map \(E \to E^*\); the skew term makes this so. The inverse function theorem, with an inverse smooth on its whole image Chapter1/SquareRootexists_openPartialHomeomorph_of_contDiffOn, makes \(C(x) = \Psi^{-1}(B(x))\) smooth near \(0\), with \(C(0) = \mathrm{id}\) and \(B(x)(v, v) = B_0(C(x)v, C(x)v)\) Chapter1/SquareRootexists_sqrt_family.
  3. \(\psi(x) = C(x - p)(x - p)\) has \(d\psi_p = C(0) = \mathrm{id}\); inverting it again gives \(\varphi\), with \(f = f(p) + B_0(\varphi, \varphi)\).
  4. Sylvester’s law of inertia in Mathlib gives an isomorphism \(e : E \to \mathbb R^n\) with \(d^2f_p(v, v) = -\sum_{i<\lambda} (ev)_i^2 + \sum_{i \ge \lambda} (ev)_i^2\), after a permutation Chapter1/MorseLemmaexists_linearEquiv_diagForm. Put \(y = e(\varphi/\sqrt2)\).
  5. On \(M\), apply this to \(f \circ \kappa_p^{-1}\) on \(\kappa_p(U \cap \operatorname{dom} \kappa_p)\): its Hessian at \(\kappa_p(p)\) is \(f_{**}\), and \(\kappa_p(p)\) is critical by §1.3. Then \(y \circ \kappa_p\) is a smooth coordinate system. \(\square\)

1.7 Non-degenerate critical points are isolated

Corollary 2.3 [V1.10]. Let \(E\) be finite-dimensional, \(f : M \to \mathbb R\) \(C^2\) at \(p\), and \(p\) a non-degenerate critical point. Some neighbourhood of \(p\) contains no other critical point. Chapter1/ManifoldMorseIsNondegenerateCriticalPointM.exists_nhds_isCriticalPointM_eq

Proof. On \(E\), \(x \mapsto df_x \in E^*\) has at \(p\) the injective, hence bounded below, derivative \(v \mapsto d^2f_p(v, \cdot)\), so \(df_x \ne 0\) for \(x \ne p\) near \(p\) Chapter1/Nondegenerateeventually_not_isCriticalPoint. On \(M\) read this in \(\kappa_p\), which is injective (§1.3). \(\square\)

Theorem [V1.11]. (i) The critical set of a \(C^1\) function on \(M\) is closed. Let \(E\) be finite-dimensional. (ii) If \(f\) is \(C^2\) on \(S \subseteq M\) and its critical points in \(S\) are non-degenerate, they form a discrete set. (iii) If \(f\) is \(C^2\) with non-degenerate critical points, a compact set contains finitely many; so does a compact \(M\) for a Morse function. Chapter1/ManifoldMorsefinite_inter_setOf_isCriticalPointM Chapter1/ManifoldMorseIsMorseFunction.finite_setOf_isCriticalPointM

Proof. (i) If \(df_{x_0} \ne 0\), the derivative of \(f \circ \kappa_{x_0}^{-1}\) is non-zero near \(\kappa_{x_0}(x_0)\) by continuity; read back by §1.3. (ii) is Corollary 2.3. (iii) The critical points in a compact \(K\) form a closed, hence compact, discrete set, which is finite; no Hausdorff hypothesis is used. \(\square\)

← 0. The path2. Sublevel sets and attached cells →

2. Sublevel sets and attached cells

This chapter proves Theorems 3.1, 3.2 and 3.5 for \(f = F|N\), with \(N \subseteq V\) a slice submanifold modelled on a finite-dimensional \(Z\) and \(F : V \to \mathbb R\) smooth (§1.1). The Morse inequalities, Theorems 17.3 and 22.1 and Bott periodicity need Theorems 3.1 and 3.2; no other main theorem needs Theorem 3.5. Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 on a Euclidean space or an abstract manifold, the Remark on p. 13, Remark 3.4 and Lemma 3.6 are not needed (the construction of Lemma 3.6 reappears in the proof of Lemma 3.7).

2.1 Sublevel sets and deformation retracts

Definition and lemma [V2.1]. For \(F : T \to \mathbb R\) on a set, \(T^c = \{x : F(x) \le c\}\). A subset \(A\) of a space \(X\) is a strong deformation retract of \(X\) if there are a continuous \(r : X \to X\) with values in \(A\) and a homotopy \(r_t\) from \(r_0 = \mathrm{id}\) to \(r_1 = r\) with \(r_t(a) = a\) for all \(t\) and \(a \in A\). If \(A \subseteq B\) and \(A\) is one of \(B\), the inclusion \(A \to B\) is a homotopy equivalence with homotopy inverse \(r_1\). Chapter2/Crossingsublevel Chapter2/CrossingIsStrongDeformationRetract Chapter2/CrossingIsStrongDeformationRetract.exists_homotopyEquiv

Proof. \(r_1 \circ i = \mathrm{id}_A\), and \(i \circ r_1 = r\) is homotopic to \(\mathrm{id}_B\). \(\square\)

Strong deformation retractions compose: if \(A \subseteq B \subseteq C\), first deform \(C\) onto \(B\) by \(s_t\), then follow \(r_t \circ s_1\) Chapter2/CellAttachIsStrongDeformationRetract.trans.

2.2 Flows

Fact (global flows, standard) [V1.14]. Let \(E\) be a complete real normed space and \(X : E \to E\) bounded and globally Lipschitz, for instance \(C^1\) and zero outside a compact set. Through each point there is a unique integral curve defined on \(\mathbb R\); the flow \(\varphi_t(x)\) has \(\varphi_0 = \mathrm{id}\), \(\varphi_{s+t} = \varphi_s \circ \varphi_t\), every integral curve is \(\gamma(t) = \varphi_{t - t_0}(\gamma(t_0))\), and \((t, x) \mapsto \varphi_t(x)\) is continuous. If \(S\) is closed and through each point of \(S\) some local solution stays in \(S\), then \(\varphi_t(S) \subseteq S\). If \(X\) is \(C^n\), \(1 \le n \le \infty\), with compact support, then \((t, x) \mapsto \varphi_t(x)\) is \(C^n\). Flow/GlobalIsBddLipschitz Flow/Globalflow Flow/GlobalIsBddLipschitz.flow_add Flow/GlobalIsBddLipschitz.flow_mem Flow/SmoothcontDiff_flow Flow/SmoothcontDiff_flow_uncurry

Proof idea. A bounded field has Picard–Lindelöf solutions on intervals of every length, which replaces Milnor’s iteration of \(\varphi_{\varepsilon_0/2}\); Grönwall gives uniqueness and continuity, and invariance holds because the times at which a flow line lies in \(S\) form a clopen set. Smoothness, which Mathlib lacks: for a Lipschitz constant below \(1\), \(\varphi_1(x)\) is the value at \(1\) of \(\Psi^{-1}\) applied to the constant curve \(x\), where \(\Psi(\gamma) = \gamma - \int_0^{\cdot} X(\gamma)\) is a \(C^n\) homeomorphism of \(C([0, 1], E)\) with invertible derivative (a Neumann series), hence with \(C^n\) inverse Flow/VolterracontDiff_voltHomeomorph_symm; then \(\varphi_t = (\varphi_{t/N})^N\), and joint smoothness follows from the flow of \((x, \tau) \mapsto (\rho(\tau) X(x), 0)\). \(\square\)

2.3 Theorem 3.1

Theorem 3.1 [V2.3]. Let \(a \le b\), and suppose that \(f^{-1}[a, b] \subseteq N\) is compact and contains no critical point of \(f\). Then a \(C^\infty\) diffeomorphism \(\Phi\) of \(N\) carries \(N^a\) onto \(N^b\), \(N^a\) is a strong deformation retract of \(N^b\), and the inclusion \(N^a \to N^b\) is a homotopy equivalence. If \(N\) is compact, \(f^{-1}[a, b]\) need not be assumed compact. Chapter2/Submanifoldtheorem_3_1_submanifold Chapter2/Submanifoldtheorem_3_1_submanifold_of_isCompact

Proof. Milnor’s, without a metric: an ambient field tangent to \(N\) replaces \(\rho \operatorname{grad} f\), and a lemma on one real function replaces his “clearly”. Let \(K = f^{-1}[a, b]\).

  1. A field. For a slice chart \(\sigma\) and \(u \in Z\), \(Y_u(y) = d(\sigma^{-1})_{\sigma(y)}(u, 0)\) is smooth on \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma\) and tangent to \(N\) along \(N\). As \(dF_q\) does not vanish on \(T_qN\) for \(q \in K\) [V1.6, §1.4], some \(Y_u\) has \(dF(Y_u) > 0\) near \(q\); a finite sum of bump functions times such fields is a smooth \(Y\), tangent to \(N\) along \(N\), with \(dF(Y) > 0\) on \(K\) Chapter2/Submanifoldexists_tangent_field. A smooth Urysohn function divided by \(dF(Y)\) is a \(\rho\) with compact support in the union \(O\) of the slice chart domains and \(\rho\, dF(Y) = 1\) on \(K\) Chapter2/Regularexists_cutoff_mul. Let \(X = \rho Y\).
  2. \(N\) is invariant. Local solutions of \(X\) read in a slice chart, mapped back by the parametrization, are integral curves in \(N\). So \(N \cup (V \setminus O)\), closed as \(N\) is closed in \(O\), is invariant (Fact), and a flow line from \(N\) cannot reach a zero of \(X\): \(\varphi_t(N) \subseteq N\) Chapter2/Submanifoldflow_mem_of_tangent. As a smooth map into \(V\) with values in \(N\) is smooth into \(N\), \(\Phi = \varphi_{b-a}|N\) is a diffeomorphism with inverse \(\varphi_{a-b}|N\).
  3. One crossing. \(g(t) = f(\varphi_t(x))\) is continuous, with \(g' = dF(X) = 1\) where \(g \in [a, b]\). By continuous induction, if \(g(s) \ge c \in [a, b]\) then \(g \ge c\) after \(s\), and if \(g(s) \in [a, b]\) then \(g(s + \tau) = g(s) + \tau\) for \(a - g(s) \le \tau \le b - g(s)\) Chapter2/CrossingUnitSpeedInSlab.eq_add. A flow line crosses the slab once, upwards, at unit speed, so \(\varphi_{c'-c}(N^c) = N^{c'}\) for \(a \le c \le c' \le b\) Chapter2/CrossingIsSlabFlow.image_sublevel.
  4. The deformation. Milnor’s two-case \(r_t\) is \(r_t(x) = \varphi_{t \min(0,\, a - f(x))}(x)\), continuous in \((t, x)\). It fixes \(N^a\), and \(f(r_t(x)) = f(x) + t(a - f(x))\) on the slab, so \(r_t(N^b) \subseteq N^b\) and \(r_1(N^b) \subseteq N^a\) Chapter2/CrossingIsSlabFlow.isStrongDeformationRetract. §2.1 finishes; for compact \(N\), \(K\) is closed in \(N\). \(\square\)

2.4 A cell inside a space

Lemma D [V2.7]. Let \(W\) be Hausdorff, \(j : A \to W\) a closed embedding, \(D\) compact, \(\chi : D \to W\) continuous and injective, \(i : S \to D\), and \(\varphi : S \to A\) with \(j\varphi = \chi i\). If \(W = j(A) \cup \chi(D)\) and \(\chi(d) \in j(A)\) only for \(d \in i(S)\), then \(W\) is the pushout of \(A \xleftarrow{\varphi} S \xrightarrow{i} D\). Hence, if \(A\) is closed in a Hausdorff space \(M\) and \(\chi : D^n \to M\) is continuous and injective with \(\chi(z) \in A\) iff \(|z| = 1\), then \(A \cup \chi(D^n)\) is \(A \cup_\varphi e^n\) [V1.2, §1.1] with \(\varphi = \chi|S^{n-1}\) injective. If moreover \(A = M^a\) for a continuous \(f\), \(a \le b\), \(\chi(D^n) \subseteq M^b\), and \(M^a \cup \chi(D^n)\) is a strong deformation retract of \(M^b\), then \(M^b\) is homotopy equivalent to \(M^a \cup_\varphi e^n\). Chapter2/CellAdjunctionisPushout_of_cell Chapter2/CellPatchexists_isPushout_union_cell_of_t2 Chapter2/CellPatchexists_homotopyEquiv_pushout_of_cell

Proof. \(j\) and \(\chi\) are homeomorphisms onto closed images. Maps \(a\) on \(A\) and \(d\) on \(D\) with \(a\varphi = di\) glue to \(a j^{-1}\) on \(j(A)\) and \(d\chi^{-1}\) on \(\chi(D)\), which agree on the overlap by the hypothesis on \(i(S)\); the result is continuous by the pasting lemma and unique. The last claim adds §2.1. \(\square\)

2.5 Theorem 3.2

Let \(X\), \(Y\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces, \(\xi(x, y) = |x|^2\), \(\eta(x, y) = |y|^2\). For \(f : M \to \mathbb R\) on a space, a Morse patch at \(p\) is an open partial homeomorphism \(\varphi : M \to X \times Y\) with \(\varphi(p) = 0\) and \(f = c - \xi\varphi + \eta\varphi\) on its domain, \(c = f(p)\) Chapter2/CellPatchIsMorsePatch. Milnor’s \(\mu\) for \(\epsilon > 0\) is smooth with \(\mu(0) > \epsilon\), \(\mu = 0\) on \([2\epsilon, \infty)\) and \(-1 < \mu' \le 0\) Chapter2/CellModelIsMilnorMu. Milnor does not show that one exists; \(\mu(r) = \tfrac34 \int_r^{2\epsilon} \beta\) is one, for a smooth \(\beta : \mathbb R \to [0, 1]\) equal to \(1\) below \(\tfrac32\epsilon\) and \(0\) above \(2\epsilon\) Chapter2/CellModelisMilnorMu_milnorMu. Then \(\mu \ge 0\), \(\mu\) decreases, and \(s + \mu(s)\) increases. Put \(\tilde f = f - \mu(\xi\varphi + 2\eta\varphi)\) on \(\operatorname{dom}\varphi\) and \(\tilde f = f\) elsewhere; \(\tilde f = f\) off the ellipsoid \(\varphi^{-1}\{\xi + 2\eta \le 2\epsilon\}\). The cell is \(e = \varphi^{-1}\{\xi \le \epsilon,\ y = 0\}\). In coordinates:

  • Assertion 1: \(\tilde f \le c + \epsilon\) iff \(f \le c + \epsilon\), as \(\tilde f \le f\) and both hold on the ellipsoid.
  • Assertion 2: \(d\tilde f = -(1 + \mu')\, d\xi + (1 - 2\mu')\, d\eta\) vanishes only at \(0\) (evaluate on \((x, 0)\) and \((0, y)\)).
  • On \(e\), \(\tilde f = c - \xi - \mu(\xi) \le c - \mu(0) < c - \epsilon\), and \(e \cap M^{c-\epsilon} = \{\xi = \epsilon,\ y = 0\}\).
  • Assertion 4: Milnor’s three cases are one formula, \(r_t(x, y) = (x, \sigma_t y)\) with \(\sigma_t = 1 - t + t\sqrt{\min(1, (\xi - \epsilon)/\eta)}\), where \(0/0 = 0\) and \(\sqrt s = 0\) for \(s < 0\). As \(0 \le \sigma_t \le 1\), \(r_t\) keeps \(\xi\) and does not increase \(\eta\), nor \(\tilde f\); it fixes \(M^{c-\epsilon} = \{\eta + \epsilon \le \xi\}\) and \(e\); \(r_1\) lands in \(M^{c-\epsilon} \cup e\); and \(r_t\) is continuous, also where \(\eta = 0\), since it moves no point farther from such a point. Transported by \(\varphi\) and extended by the identity, it stays in the chart on \(\tilde f^{-1}(-\infty, c - \epsilon]\) and is continuous there if \(M\) is Hausdorff, the ellipsoid being compact, hence closed. So \(M^{c-\epsilon} \cup e\) is a strong deformation retract of \(\tilde f^{-1}(-\infty, c - \epsilon]\) Chapter2/CellPatchisStrongDeformationRetract_patch_handle.

Theorem 3.2 in a patch [V2.8]. Let \(M\) be Hausdorff, \(\varphi\) a Morse patch at \(p\) whose image contains \(\{\xi + \eta \le 2\epsilon\}\), \(\epsilon > 0\), \(\mu\) as above, and \(\iota\) a linear isometry of \(X\) onto \(\mathbb R^\lambda\). If \(\tilde f^{-1}(-\infty, c - \epsilon]\) is a strong deformation retract of \(M^{c+\epsilon}\) (Assertion 3), then \(\chi(z) = \varphi^{-1}(\sqrt\epsilon\, \iota^{-1} z, 0)\) is continuous and injective on \(D^\lambda\), \(\chi(z) \in M^{c-\epsilon}\) iff \(|z| = 1\), \(\chi(D^\lambda) \subseteq M^{c+\epsilon}\), and \(M^{c-\epsilon} \cup \chi(D^\lambda)\) is a strong deformation retract of \(M^{c+\epsilon}\). Chapter2/CellPatchpatch_theorem_3_2

Proof. \(f(\chi(z)) = c - \epsilon|z|^2\); compose Assertion 3 with Assertion 4 (§2.1). \(\square\)

Theorem 3.2 [V2.8]. Let \(p \in N\) be a non-degenerate critical point of \(f\) of index \(\lambda\), \(c = f(p)\), and suppose that for some \(\epsilon_0 > 0\) the set \(f^{-1}[c - \epsilon_0, c + \epsilon_0]\) is compact with no critical point but \(p\). There is \(\epsilon_1 > 0\) such that for every \(\epsilon \in (0, \epsilon_1]\) there is a \(\chi : D^\lambda \to N\) with the four properties of the patch theorem, \(N\) in place of \(M\); and \(N^{c+\epsilon}\) is homotopy equivalent to \(N^{c-\epsilon} \cup_\varphi e^\lambda\) for an injective \(\varphi\). Chapter2/CellAttachSubmanifoldtheorem_3_2_submanifold Chapter2/CellAttachSubmanifoldtheorem_3_2_attach_submanifold

Proof.

  1. The lemma of Morse on \(N\) [V1.8, §1.6], inside a slice chart \(\sigma\), with the coordinates split after the \(\lambda\)-th, gives a Morse patch \(\psi\) that is a smooth coordinate system Chapter2/CellAttachSubmanifoldexists_isMorsePatch_submanifold. If its image contains the ball of radius \(r\), let \(\epsilon_1 = \min(\epsilon_0, r^2/4)\).
  2. \(\tilde f\) is smooth, the correction vanishing off the closed ellipsoid, and has the critical points of \(f\), by Assertion 2 read in \(\psi\) (§1.3) Chapter2/CellAttachSubmanifoldisCriticalPointM_patchF_iff.
  3. Theorem 3.1 is for restrictions, so \(\tilde f\) is made one, a step Milnor does not need. The correction \(b\) vanishes off the ellipsoid, a compact subset of \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma\); for a cut-off \(\theta\) equal to \(1\) there, \(B(y) = \theta(y)\, b(x(\sigma(y)_Z))\) is smooth with \(B|N = b\) Chapter2/CellAttachSubmanifoldexists_contDiff_comp_val_eq_of_chart.
  4. Assertion 3. \(\tilde f^{-1}[c - \epsilon, c + \epsilon]\) lies in \(f^{-1}[c - \epsilon_0, c + \epsilon_0]\) (by \(\tilde f \le f\) and Assertion 1), so it is compact; its only candidate critical point is \(p\), but \(\tilde f(p) = c - \mu(0) < c - \epsilon\). Theorem 3.1 for \(F - B\) makes \(\tilde f^{-1}(-\infty, c - \epsilon]\) a strong deformation retract of \(\tilde f^{-1}(-\infty, c + \epsilon] = N^{c+\epsilon}\).
  5. Apply the patch theorem (\(\lambda \le \dim Z\) gives \(\iota\)), then Lemma D. \(\square\)

2.6 Several critical points on one level

Remark 3.3 [V2.9]. Let \(S\) be a finite set of non-degenerate critical points of \(f\), all at the level \(c\), and suppose that for some \(\epsilon_0 > 0\) the set \(f^{-1}[c - \epsilon_0, c + \epsilon_0]\) is compact with all its critical points in \(S\). There is \(\epsilon_1 > 0\) such that for every \(\epsilon \in (0, \epsilon_1]\) there are maps \(\chi_p : D^{\lambda_p} \to N\), \(p \in S\), \(\lambda_p\) the index of \(p\), continuous and injective, with \(\chi_p(z) \in N^{c-\epsilon}\) iff \(|z| = 1\), images in \(N^{c+\epsilon}\) and pairwise disjoint, such that \(N^{c-\epsilon} \cup \bigcup_p \chi_p(D^{\lambda_p})\) is a strong deformation retract of \(N^{c+\epsilon}\). Chapter2/SeveralCriticalremark_3_3_submanifold

Proof. \(N\) is Hausdorff, so the points of \(S\) have Morse patches with disjoint domains Chapter2/SeveralCriticalexists_isMorsePatch_submanifold_subset, and one \(\epsilon\) serves all. Subtract the extended corrections \(B_p\) one at a time. By induction on the set \(s\) already subtracted Chapter2/SeveralCriticalmulti_induction, \(F_s = F - \sum_{p \in s} B_p\) satisfies Assertions 1, 2 and 4 of §2.5, since each step is Milnor’s modification of \(F_s|N\) in a patch where \(F_s = F\). For Assertion 4 the earlier deformation is first extended by the identity over the new cell: if \(A\) is a strong deformation retract of \(B\), with \(B\), \(C\) closed and \(B \cap C \subseteq A\), then \(A \cup C\) is one of \(B \cup C\) Chapter2/SeveralCriticalIsStrongDeformationRetract.union_of_isClosed. Assertion 3 for \(F_S\) is as in §2.5. \(\square\)

2.7 Cell complexes and Lemma 3.7

Definition [V2.11]. \(K\) is an iterated adjunction space with cells \((\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)\) if it is obtained from \(\emptyset\) by attaching a \(\lambda_1\)-cell, then a \(\lambda_2\)-cell, and so on, each along an arbitrary continuous map into the space built so far [V1.2, §1.1]. A space has the homotopy type of a finite cell complex with cells \((\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)\) if it is homotopy equivalent to such a \(K\). Chapter2/CWTypeIsCellAttachment Chapter2/CWTypeIsFiniteCellComplexType

Unlike Milnor’s CW-complexes, the attaching maps need not be cellular: Mathlib has no cellular approximation.

Lemma 3.7 [V2.14]. Let \(\varphi : S^{n-1} \to X\) be continuous and \(f : X \to Y\) a homotopy equivalence. The map \(F : X \cup_\varphi e^n \to Y \cup_{f\varphi} e^n\) which is \(f\) on \(X\) and the identity on the cell is a homotopy equivalence. And for maps with \(LF \simeq \mathrm{id}\) and \(FR \simeq \mathrm{id}\), also \(RF \simeq \mathrm{id}\). Chapter2/Attachinglemma_3_7 Chapter2/Attachinghomotopic_of_leftInv_rightInv

Proof. The second claim: \(L \simeq L(FR) = (LF)R \simeq R\), so \(RF \simeq LF \simeq \mathrm{id}\). A homotopy out of \(X \cup_\varphi e^n\) may be given on \(X\) and on \(D^n\) compatibly, because \([0, 1] \times (\text{quotient map})\) is a quotient map (\([0, 1]\) is locally compact) Chapter2/AttachingcellHomotopy. On the cell, write \(z = tu\), \(|u| = 1\); every map below is radial: \(tu \mapsto (t/a)u\) for \(t \le a\) and \(tu \mapsto \Psi(t, u) \in X\) for \(t \ge a\), where \(\Psi(a, u) = \varphi(u)\) Chapter2/Attachingradial.

  1. For a homotopy \(\varphi_s\) from \(\varphi_0\) to \(\varphi_1\), Milnor’s \(k : X \cup_{\varphi_0} e^n \to X \cup_{\varphi_1} e^n\) is the identity on \(X\) and radial with \(a = \tfrac12\), \(\Psi(t, u) = \varphi_{2-2t}(u)\); \(\ell\) is \(k\) for the reversed homotopy, and \(\ell k \simeq \mathrm{id}\) through the radial maps with \(a = (1 + 3\tau)/4\) and \(\Psi(t, u) = \varphi_{\min(4(t - a),\, 2 - 2t)}(u)\) Chapter2/Attachinglemma36Homotopy.
  2. Let \(g\) be a homotopy inverse of \(f\), \(h_\tau\) a homotopy from \(gf\) to \(\mathrm{id}_X\), \(G\) the analogue of \(F\) for \(g\), and \(k\) as in 1 for \(h_\tau\varphi\). Then \(kGF \simeq \mathrm{id}\), through \(h_\tau\) on \(X\) and the radial maps with \(a = (1 + \tau)/2\), \(\Psi(t, u) = h_{2-2t+\tau}(\varphi(u))\) Chapter2/Attachinglemma37Homotopy.
  3. So \(k\) has left inverse \(\ell\) and right inverse \(GF\), whence \(GFk \simeq \mathrm{id}\). The same with \(f\), \(g\) exchanged gives \(G\) a left inverse, while \(Fk\) is a right one: \(FkG \simeq \mathrm{id}\). Thus \(kG\) is a two-sided homotopy inverse of \(F\). \(\square\)

2.8 Theorem 3.5

Theorem (the Remark on p. 24, at regular values) [V2.15]. Let \(N\) be compact, all critical points of \(f\) non-degenerate, and \(a\) not a critical value. The critical points \(p\) with \(f(p) < a\) can be listed without repetition as \(p_1, \dots, p_j\), with \(f(p_1) \le \dots \le f(p_j)\), so that \(N^a\) has the homotopy type of a finite cell complex with cells \((\lambda(p_1), \dots, \lambda(p_j))\), \(\lambda(p)\) the index. Chapter2/CWTypeisFiniteCellComplexType_sublevel'

Proof. \(f\) is a Morse function on the compact \(N\), so it has finitely many critical points [V1.11, §1.7]. Induct on their number below \(a\). If there is none, \(N^a = \emptyset\): a global minimum is a critical point Chapter2/CWTypeisCriticalPointM_of_forall_le, and \(a\) is regular. Otherwise let \(c\) be the largest critical value below \(a\), \(S\) the critical points at level \(c\), and \(a' < c\) a regular value above all smaller critical values. Remark 3.3, with \(\epsilon_0 = \min(c - a', a - c)\), gives \(\epsilon \le \epsilon_0/2\) and disjoint cells, and Theorem 3.1 makes \(N^{a'} \to N^{c-\epsilon}\) and \(N^{c+\epsilon} \to N^a\) homotopy equivalences; \(N^{a'}\) is handled by induction. The cells are attached one at a time: by Lemma D each meets the closed set built so far exactly in its boundary sphere, and attaching a cell preserves the property, since \(X \cup_\varphi e^n \simeq K \cup_{h\varphi} e^n\) for \(h : X \simeq K\) by Lemma 3.7 Chapter2/CWTypeisFiniteCellComplexType_union_cells Chapter2/CWTypeIsFiniteCellComplexType.sublevel_step_finset. \(\square\)

Theorem 3.5 [V2.12]. Let \(N\) be compact and all critical points of \(f\) non-degenerate. The critical points can be listed without repetition as \(p_1, \dots, p_k\), with \(f(p_1) \le \dots \le f(p_k)\), so that \(N\) has the homotopy type of a finite cell complex with cells \((\lambda(p_1), \dots, \lambda(p_k))\); in particular of one whose number of cells of dimension \(\lambda\) is, for every \(\lambda\), the number \(C_\lambda\) of critical points of index \(\lambda\). Chapter2/CWTypetheorem_3_5' Chapter2/CWTypetheorem_3_5_count'

Proof. Take \(a > \max f\) in the previous theorem, so \(N^a = N\); count the entries. \(\square\)

3. Morse functions exist

This chapter proves Theorem 6.6: on a slice submanifold \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^n\), for almost every \(p\) the function \(L_p(q) = \|q - p\|^2\) is a Morse function. The same argument shows that a generic linear perturbation of a smooth function on a manifold embedded in \(\mathbb R^n\) is a Morse function (§3.3); only Theorem 22.1, and through it Bott periodicity (Theorems 23.5, 24.7), needs this. Principal curvatures, Lemmas 6.3 and 6.9, Assertion 6.4, Corollaries 6.7 and 6.8 and Whitney’s embedding theorem are not needed.

In §§3.1–3.3, \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^n\) is a slice submanifold modelled on \(\mathbb R^k\) with complement \(\mathbb R^w\) [V1.6, §1.4], not necessarily closed or compact.

3.1 The normal bundle and focal points

Fact (Sard’s theorem) (companion volume). Let \(E, F\) be finite-dimensional real normed spaces, \(U \subseteq E\) open, \(f : E \to F\) smooth on \(U\), \(\mu\) a Haar measure on \(F\). Then \(f(\{x \in U : df_x \text{ not onto}\})\) is \(\mu\)-null. Milnor/Chapter3/Sardsard

Theorem 6.1 [V4.3]. Let \(X\) be a second countable smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional space, \(F, \mu\) as above, \(U \subseteq X\) open and \(f : X \to F\) smooth on \(U\). Then \(f(\{x \in U : df_x \text{ not onto}\})\) is \(\mu\)-null. Chapter4/Sardmeasure_image_inter_critPoints_eq_zero

Proof. Countably many charts \(\varphi\) cover \(U\); a critical point of \(f\) is one of \(f \circ \varphi^{-1}\) by the chain rule. Apply Sard to each \(f \circ \varphi^{-1}\). \(\square\)

Definition (normal bundle, endpoint maps) [V4.1]. If \(M \ne \emptyset\) then \(k + w = n\), by the dimensions in a slice chart Chapter4/Focalslice_dim_add_eq_of_nonempty. The normal bundle is \(N = \{(q, v) \in M \times \mathbb R^n : v \perp T_qM\}\) Milnor/Chapter8/NormalBundlenormalBundleSet. For \(\Gamma : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^n\) put \(E_\Gamma(q, v) = \Gamma(q) + v\) on \(N\) Chapter4/NormalBundlenormalEnd; Milnor’s endpoint map is \(E = E_{\mathrm{id}}\).

Fact (the normal bundle is a manifold) (companion volume). If \(k + w = n\), \(N\) is a slice submanifold of \(\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^n\) of dimension \(n\) Milnor/Chapter8/NormalBundleisSliceSubmanifold_normalBundle. Near \((q, v)\) it is the zero set of \(\Theta(a, b) = ((\sigma a)_2, B(a)b)\), \(\sigma\) the slice chart of \(M\) at \(q\) and \(B(a)\) the adjoint of the derivative of \(u \mapsto \sigma^{-1}(u, 0)\) at \((\sigma a)_1\); \(d\Theta\) is onto, and \(T_{(q,v)}N = \ker d\Theta\) Milnor/Chapter8/LocalSliceIsSliceSubmanifold.range_mfderiv_val_eq_ker.

Definition (fundamental forms) [V4.5]. For \(q \in M\) let \(x(u) = \sigma^{-1}(u, 0)\), \(x(u_q) = q\) (Milnor’s coordinates), and \(dx\), \(d^2x\) its derivatives at \(u_q\); \(dx\) is injective. On \(\mathbb R^k\) put \(g(\xi, \eta) = \langle dx\,\xi, dx\,\eta\rangle\), \(\ell_v(\xi, \eta) = \langle v, d^2x(\xi, \eta)\rangle\) and, for \(T\) linear, \(B_{T,v}(\xi, \eta) = \langle T\,dx\,\xi, dx\,\eta\rangle - \ell_v(\xi, \eta)\); so \(B_{\mathrm{id},v} = g - \ell_v\). Chapter4/NormalBundlenormalForm

Lemma (the Jacobian of \(E_\Gamma\)) [V4.8]. Let \(k + w = n\) and \((q, v) \in N\).

  1. \((a, b)\) is tangent to \(N\) at \((q, v)\) iff \(a = dx\,\xi\) for some \(\xi\) and \(\langle b, dx\,\eta\rangle + \langle v, d^2x(\xi, \eta)\rangle = 0\) for all \(\eta\). Chapter4/NormalBundlemem_range_mfd_val_normalBundle_iff
  2. If \(\Gamma\) is differentiable at \(q\), \(dE_\Gamma\) at \((q, v)\) is \((a, b) \mapsto d\Gamma_q a + b\) on \(T_{(q,v)}N\), with kernel of dimension \(\operatorname{nullity} B_{d\Gamma_q, v}\) Chapter4/NormalBundlefinrank_ker_mfd_normalEnd. In particular \(\dim \ker dE_{(q,v)} = \operatorname{nullity}(g - \ell_v)\) Chapter4/FocalendpointNullity_eq_nullity.

Proof. (1) As \(\sigma \circ x = (\cdot, 0)\), \((d\sigma\,a)_2 = 0\) iff \(a = dx\,\xi\). And \(\langle B(q)b, \eta\rangle = \langle b, dx\,\eta\rangle\), \(dB_q(a) = d^2x((d\sigma\,a)_1, \cdot)^\dagger\), so the second component of \(d\Theta(a, b)\), paired with \(\eta\), is the displayed expression. (2) The chain rule; a tangent pair with \(d\Gamma_q a + b = 0\) has \(a = dx\,\xi\), \(b = -d\Gamma_q\,dx\,\xi\), and (1) reads \(B_{d\Gamma_q, v}(\xi, \cdot) = 0\); \(\xi \mapsto (dx\,\xi, -d\Gamma_q\,dx\,\xi)\) is injective. \(\square\)

Definition (focal points) [V4.2]. Let \(k + w = n\). The nullity of \(E\) at \(z \in N\) is \(\dim \ker dE_z\), \(T_zN\) read in a chart Chapter4/FocalendpointNullity. A point \(e\) is a focal point of \((M, q)\) of multiplicity \(\mu\) if \((q, e - q) \in N\) and the nullity there is \(\mu > 0\) Chapter4/FocalIsFocalPointMult; a focal point of \(M\) if it is one of some \((M, q)\) Chapter4/FocalfocalSet. As \(\dim N = n\), the nullity is positive iff \(dE_z\) is not onto Chapter4/FocalendpointNullity_pos_iff, so the focal points of \(M\) are the critical values of \(E\) Chapter4/FocalfocalSet_eq_image_critPoints.

Corollary 6.2 [V4.4]. If \(k + w = n\), the focal points of \(M\) form a null set for every Haar measure. Chapter4/Focalmeasure_focalSet_eq_zero

Proof. \(E\) is smooth and \(N \subseteq \mathbb R^{2n}\) second countable; Theorem 6.1. \(\square\)

3.2 Theorem 6.6

Lemma (critical points and Hessian of \(L_p\)) [V4.10]. \(q \in M\) is a critical point of \(L_p\) iff \((q, p - q) \in N\); and at every \(q \in M\), \(\operatorname{Hess}(L_p \circ x)(u_q) = 2(g - \ell_{p-q})\). Chapter4/FocalisCriticalPointM_normSq_sub_iff_mem_normalBundleSet Chapter4/Focalhessian_normSq_sub_xParam

Proof. \(dL_p = 2\langle y - p, \cdot\rangle\) vanishes on \(T_qM\) iff \(p - q \perp T_qM\); and \(\operatorname{Hess}(L_p \circ x) = 2(\langle dx\,\xi, dx\,\eta\rangle + \langle d^2x(\xi, \eta), x - p\rangle)\) by the second-order chain rule [V1.6, §1.4]. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.5 [V4.11]. Let \(k + w = n\), \(q \in M\). If \((q, p - q) \in N\), the nullity of \(L_p\) at \(q\) equals the nullity of \(E\) at \((q, p - q)\). Hence \(p\) is a focal point of \((M, q)\) of multiplicity \(\mu\) iff \(q\) is a critical point of \(L_p\) of nullity \(\mu > 0\); and \(q\) is a degenerate critical point of \(L_p\) iff \(p\) is a focal point of \((M, q)\). Chapter4/FocalnullityM_normSq_sub_eq_endpointNullity Chapter4/FocalisFocalPointMult_iff Chapter4/FocalisDegenerate_normSq_sub_iff_isFocalPoint

Proof. At a critical point the nullity is read in \(x\) [V1.6, §1.4]: it is that of \(2(g - \ell_{p-q})\), hence of \(g - \ell_{p-q}\), hence of \(E\) [V4.8, §3.1]. Non-degenerate means nullity \(0\) [V1.3, §1.2]. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.6 [V4.12]. For every slice submanifold \(M \subseteq \mathbb R^n\) and every Haar measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), \(L_p\) is a Morse function on \(M\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(p\). Chapter4/Focalae_isMorseFunction_normSq_sub

Proof. Let \(M \ne \emptyset\), so \(k + w = n\). If the smooth \(L_p\) is not a Morse function, it has a degenerate critical point \(q\), and \(p\) is a focal point of \((M, q)\) (Lemma 6.5) Chapter4/Focalmem_focalSet_of_not_isMorseFunction. Such \(p\) form a null set (Corollary 6.2). \(\square\)

3.3 Linear perturbations

Theorem 22.1 applies [V4.22, §3.3], the formal substitute for Milnor’s Corollary 6.8, to a slice submanifold of \(V\), \(e\) being its inclusion followed by a linear isomorphism \(V \cong \mathbb R^{\dim V}\).

Theorem (generic linear perturbations) [V4.20]. For every smooth \(f : M \to \mathbb R\) and every Haar measure on \(\mathbb R^n\), \(f + \langle a, \cdot\rangle\) is a Morse function on \(M\) for almost every \(a\). Chapter4/Approximationae_isMorseFunction_add_inner

Proof. Let \(M \ne \emptyset\). For smooth \(F\) define \(-\nabla F\) by \(\langle -\nabla F(y), u\rangle = -dF_y u\); then \(\langle d(-\nabla F)_y u, u'\rangle = -d^2F_y(u, u')\).

  1. Near each point \(f\) extends to a smooth \(F\) on an open \(U \subseteq \mathbb R^n\), namely \(F(y) = f(\sigma^{-1}((\sigma y)_1, 0))\) Chapter4/Approximationexists_local_extension_of_contMDiff.
  2. Let \(q \in M \cap U\) be a degenerate critical point of \(f + \langle a, \cdot\rangle\). Then \(G = F + \langle a, \cdot\rangle\), equal to it on \(M\) near \(q\), has \(dG_q = \langle v, \cdot\rangle\), \(v = a + \nabla F(q)\), vanishing on \(T_qM\); so \((q, v) \in N\) and \(E_{-\nabla F}(q, v) = a\). And \(\operatorname{Hess}(G \circ x) = d^2F_q(dx\,\cdot, dx\,\cdot) + \ell_v = -B_{d(-\nabla F)_q, v}\) has positive nullity, being the Hessian of \(f + \langle a, \cdot\rangle\) in \(x\); by [V4.8, §3.1] \(dE_{-\nabla F}\) is not onto at \((q, v)\) Chapter4/Approximationmem_image_critPoints_of_not_isNondegenerate.
  3. Countably many such \(U\) cover \(M\). Over each, \(E_{-\nabla F}\) is smooth and its critical values, which by step 2 contain the exceptional \(a\), are null (Theorem 6.1). \(\square\)

Theorem (the image of an embedding) [V4.14]. Let \(E, F, Z, W\) be finite-dimensional real normed spaces, \(\dim Z = \dim E\), \(\dim Z + \dim W = \dim F\), \(X\) a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on \(E\), and \(e : X \to F\) smooth, a homeomorphism onto its image, with injective derivative everywhere. Then \(e(X)\) is a slice submanifold of \(F\) modelled on \(Z\) with complement \(W\), and \(e : X \to e(X)\) is a diffeomorphism. Chapter4/WhitneySliceisSliceSubmanifold_range Chapter4/WhitneySlicediffeomorphRange

Proof. Fix \(T : Z \cong E\), a chart \(\varphi\) at \(x\), and \(L : W \to F\) such that \((z, w) \mapsto de_x(Tz) + Lw\) is invertible (\(L\) onto a complement of \(\operatorname{range} de_x\)). That is the derivative of \(\Psi(z, w) = e(\varphi^{-1}(Tz)) + Lw\) at \((T^{-1}\varphi x, 0)\), so \(\Psi\) is a local diffeomorphism \(\Phi\) there Milnor/Chapter1/InverseFunctionisLocalDiffeomorphAt_of_isInvertible_mfderiv. As \(e\) is an embedding, the \(y\) with \((T^{-1}\varphi y, 0)\) in the domain of \(\Phi\) form \(e^{-1}(O)\), \(O\) open, and \(\Phi^{-1}|_O\) is a slice chart: \(\Phi^{-1}(e(y)) = (T^{-1}\varphi y, 0)\), and \(\Phi^{-1}(p) = (z, 0)\) forces \(p = e(\varphi^{-1}(Tz))\) Chapter4/WhitneySliceexists_sliceChart_range. Near \(e(x)\), \(e^{-1} = \varphi^{-1} \circ T \circ (\Phi^{-1})_1\) is smooth. \(\square\)

Lemma (invariance under diffeomorphisms) [V4.15]. Let \(g : X \to X'\) be a diffeomorphism of manifolds without boundary modelled on real normed spaces, and \(f : X \to \mathbb R\). (1) \(q\) is a critical point of \(f \circ g^{-1}\) iff \(g^{-1}q\) is one of \(f\). (2) If \(f\) is \(C^2\) at a critical point \(g^{-1}q\), the Hessian of \(f \circ g^{-1}\) at \(q\) is non-degenerate iff that of \(f\) at \(g^{-1}q\) is. (3) \(f\) is a Morse function iff \(f \circ g^{-1}\) is. Chapter4/WhitneyInvarianceisCriticalPointM_comp_symm_iff Chapter4/WhitneyInvarianceisNondegenerate_hessianM_comp_symm_iff Chapter4/WhitneyInvarianceisMorseFunction_comp_symm_iff

Proof. (1) The chain rule; where \(f\) is not differentiable, neither is \(f \circ g^{-1}\), and both derivatives are \(0\) by convention. (2) The Hessian of \(f \circ g^{-1}\) in the chart at \(q\) is that of \(f\) in the smooth coordinate system \(\mathrm{chart}_q \circ g\) Chapter4/WhitneyInvariancehessianM_comp_symm_eq, and non-degeneracy does not depend on the coordinate system [V1.5, §1.3]. (3) From (1), (2), for \(g\) and \(g^{-1}\). \(\square\)

Theorem (perturbations through an embedding) [V4.22]. Let \(X\), \(E\) and \(e\) be as in [V4.14, §3.3], with \(F = \mathbb R^n\), and \(f : X \to \mathbb R\) smooth. Then \(f + \langle a, e(\cdot)\rangle\) is a Morse function for almost every \(a\) (any Haar measure). Chapter4/Whitneyae_isMorseFunction_add_inner_comp

Proof. Let \(X \ne \emptyset\); then \(\dim E \le n\), and \(\Phi = e\) is a diffeomorphism onto the slice submanifold \(e(X)\) [V4.14, §3.3]. For almost every \(a\), \(f \circ \Phi^{-1} + \langle a, \cdot\rangle\) is a Morse function on \(e(X)\) [V4.20, §3.3], hence so is its composite with \(\Phi\), \(f + \langle a, e(\cdot)\rangle\) [V4.15, §3.3]. \(\square\)

← 2. Sublevel sets and attached cells4. Homology and the Morse inequalities →

4. Homology and the Morse inequalities

This chapter proves Theorem 5.2: for a function \(f = F|_N\) with non-degenerate critical points on a compact slice submanifold \(N \subseteq V\), and any field \(\mathbb k\), the Betti numbers \(b_\lambda = \dim H_\lambda(N; \mathbb k)\) satisfy \(b_\lambda \le C_\lambda\) and \(\sum_i (-1)^i b_i = \sum_\lambda (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda\), \(C_\lambda\) the number of critical points of index \(\lambda\). The algebra is proved for an abstract homology of a filtration (§4.1); singular homology, which the formalization had to build, is one (§§4.2–4.3); the sublevel sets supply the filtration and Chapter 2 the homology of its steps (§4.4). The strong inequalities \((4_\lambda)\), Lemma 5.3, Corollary 5.4, the lacunary principle, the Mayer–Vietoris sequence, the homology of spheres, abstract compact manifolds and the examples are not needed.

4.1 The algebra of a filtration

Definition (long exact sequences) [V3.9]. Over a field \(\mathbb k\), a long exact sequence consists of vector spaces \(A_i, B_i, C_i\) (\(i \in \mathbb N\)) and linear maps \(f_i : A_i \to B_i\), \(g_i : B_i \to C_i\), \(\delta_i : C_{i+1} \to A_i\) with \(\ker g_i = \operatorname{im} f_i\), \(\ker \delta_i = \operatorname{im} g_{i+1}\), \(\ker f_i = \operatorname{im} \delta_i\), and \(g_0\) onto Chapter3/InequalitiesLongExactSeq. For \(d : \mathbb N \to \mathbb Z\) let \(\operatorname{alt}_n(d) = \sum_{i \le n} (-1)^{n-i} d_i\) Chapter3/InequalitiesaltSum.

Lemma (dimensions in a long exact sequence) [V3.10].

  1. If \(A_i\) and \(C_i\) are finite-dimensional, so is \(B_i\). Chapter3/InequalitiesLongExactSeq.finiteDimensional_middle

If all the spaces are finite-dimensional:

  1. \(\dim B_i \le \dim A_i + \dim C_i\) Chapter3/InequalitiesLongExactSeq.finrank_le;
  2. if \(C_{N+1} = 0\), then \(\operatorname{alt}_N(\dim B) = \operatorname{alt}_N(\dim A) + \operatorname{alt}_N(\dim C)\) Chapter3/InequalitiesLongExactSeq.altSum_eq_of_finrank_eq_zero.

Proof. (1) \(A_i \to B_i \to \operatorname{im} g_i \to 0\) is exact and \(\operatorname{im} g_i \subseteq C_i\). (2) Rank–nullity for \(g_i\). (3) Rank–nullity at the three kinds of places gives \(\dim A_i = \operatorname{rk} f_i + \operatorname{rk}\delta_i\), \(\dim B_i = \operatorname{rk} g_i + \operatorname{rk} f_i\), \(\dim C_{i+1} = \operatorname{rk}\delta_i + \operatorname{rk} g_{i+1}\), \(\dim C_0 = \operatorname{rk} g_0\). So \(e_i = \dim A_i - \dim B_i + \dim C_i\) has \(e_0 = \operatorname{rk}\delta_0\) and \(e_{i+1} = \operatorname{rk}\delta_{i+1} + \operatorname{rk}\delta_i\), and \(\operatorname{alt}_N(e)\) telescopes to \(\operatorname{rk}\delta_N\) Chapter3/InequalitiesLongExactSeq.finrank_range_δ, which is \(0\). \(\square\)

Definition (homology of a filtration) [V3.9]. For a preorder \(\iota\), a homology of a filtration is a family of \(\mathbb k\)-vector spaces \(H(i, a, b)\) (\(i \in \mathbb N\), \(a, b \in \iota\); read \(H_i(X_b, X_a)\)), finite-dimensional for \(a \le b\), with, for each \(a \le b \le c\), a long exact sequence with \(A_i = H(i, a, b)\), \(B_i = H(i, a, c)\), \(C_i = H(i, b, c)\) Chapter3/InequalitiesFiltrationHomology. Nothing else is assumed. The Morse numbers of a chain \(X_0 \le \dots \le X_n\) are \(C_i = \sum_{k < n} \dim H(i, X_k, X_{k+1})\) Chapter3/InequalitiesmorseNumber. For \(\iota = \mathbb N\) the finiteness need only be assumed for the steps \(H(i, k, k+1)\) and for \(H(i, k, k)\): induction on \(b\) with Lemma (1) Chapter3/InequalitiesFiltrationHomology.ofSteps.

Definition (subadditive functions) [V3.7]. \(S : \iota \times \iota \to \mathbb Z\) is subadditive if \(S(a, c) \le S(a, b) + S(b, c)\) whenever \(a \le b \le c\) Chapter3/InequalitiesIsSubadditive.

Lemma 5.1 [V3.8]. If \(S\) is subadditive and \(X_0 \le \dots \le X_n\), \(n \ge 1\), then \(S(X_0, X_n) \le \sum_{k<n} S(X_k, X_{k+1})\). Chapter3/InequalitiesIsSubadditive.le_sum

Proof. Induction on \(n\), using \(S\) only on the triples \(X_0 \le X_m \le X_{m+1}\) Chapter3/Inequalitiesle_sum_of_chain; with equality on these triples the same induction gives equality Chapter3/Inequalitieseq_sum_of_chain. \(\square\)

Hidden hypothesis. \(n \ge 1\): for \(n = 0\) the claim is \(S(X_0, X_0) \le 0\), whereas subadditivity gives \(S(X, X) \ge 0\).

Lemma [V3.10]. In a homology of a filtration, \((a, b) \mapsto \dim H(\lambda, a, b)\) is subadditive, by Lemma (2). Chapter3/InequalitiesFiltrationHomology.isSubadditive_finrank

Theorem 5.2 for a filtration [V3.11]. Given a homology of a filtration and a chain \(X_0 \le \dots \le X_n\), \(n \ge 1\), let \(b_i = \dim H(i, X_0, X_n)\).

  1. \(b_\lambda \le C_\lambda\) for every \(\lambda\). Chapter3/InequalitiesFiltrationHomology.finrank_le_morseNumber
  2. If \(H(N+1, X_k, X_{k+1}) = 0\) for all \(k < n\), then \(\sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i b_i = \sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i C_i\). Chapter3/InequalitiesFiltrationHomology.sum_neg_one_pow_finrank_eq
  3. Let \(P\) be a finite set with maps \(\operatorname{ind}, \operatorname{step} : P \to \mathbb N\), \(\operatorname{step} < n\), such that \(\dim H(i, X_k, X_{k+1}) = \#\{p : \operatorname{step} p = k,\ \operatorname{ind} p = i\}\) for all \(k < n\) and all \(i\) (the cell hypothesis). Then \(C_i = \#\{p : \operatorname{ind} p = i\}\). Chapter3/InequalitiesmorseNumber_eq_card

Proof. (1) Lemma 5.1. (2) Put \(\chi_N(a, b) = \sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i \dim H(i, a, b) = (-1)^N \operatorname{alt}_N(\dim H(\cdot, a, b))\) Chapter3/Inequalitiessum_neg_one_pow_mul_eq. On a triple \(X_0 \le X_m \le X_{m+1}\) the third pair is a step, so Lemma (3) makes \(\chi_N\) additive there; the equality case of Lemma 5.1 and an exchange of finite sums conclude. (3) Group the points of index \(i\) by their step. \(\square\)

Milnor needs one critical point per step, hence distinct critical values; the cell hypothesis allows several.

4.2 Singular homology

Mathlib has singular chains, absolute singular homology and its homotopy invariance, and the long exact sequence of a short exact sequence of complexes; the rest was built. Coefficients are a commutative ring \(R\) (a field \(\mathbb k\) from §4.3 on); the spaces are subsets of a topological space, \(H_n(B, A)\) is written for \(A \subseteq B\), and the spaces must lie in the universe of \(R\), a formality of type theory.

Fact (relative homology and the pair) [V3.26] (standard). For \(A \subseteq X\), \(C(A) \to C(X)\) is injective; the relative chains \(C(X, A)\) are its cokernel and \(H_n(X, A)\) their homology, functorial in maps of pairs Homology/RelativerelChains Homology/RelativerelHomology. The connecting map \(\partial\) of \(0 \to C(A) \to C(X) \to C(X, A) \to 0\) Homology/RelativerelShortComplex_shortExact Homology/Relativerelδ makes \(H_n(A) \to H_n(X) \to H_n(X, A) \xrightarrow{\partial} H_{n-1}(A) \to H_{n-1}(X)\) a complex, exact at \(H_n(X)\) and \(H_n(X, A)\), with \(H_0(X) \to H_0(X, A)\) onto Homology/RelativerelHomology_exact₂ Homology/RelativerelHomology_exact₃ Homology/Relativeepi_homologyMap_relπ_zero. Hence:

  • a map of pairs inducing isomorphisms on the homology of both spaces induces isomorphisms on relative homology Homology/RelativeisIso_relHomology_map; \(H_n(X, A) = 0\) if \(A = X\) Homology/RelativeisZero_relHomology_of_isIso;
  • if \(A \subseteq B \subseteq X\) and \(B\) is a strong deformation retract of \(X\) [V2.1, §2.1], then \(H_n(B, A) \cong H_n(X, A)\) and \(H_n(X, B) = 0\) Homology/RelativeRetractisIso_relHomology_map_of_isStrongDeformationRetract Homology/RelativeRetractisZero_relHomology_of_isStrongDeformationRetract.

Idea. Mathlib’s homology sequence; at degree \(0\) no differential leaves \(C_0\). Then the five lemma; the inclusion of a strong deformation retract is a homotopy equivalence, and Mathlib’s homotopy invariance applies.

Fact (the triple) [V3.27] (standard). For \(A \subseteq B \subseteq D\) Homology/TripleTopTriple.ofSubsets, \(0 \to C(B, A) \to C(D, A) \to C(D, B) \to 0\) is exact Homology/TripleTopTriple.shortComplex_shortExact, and its connecting map Homology/TripleTopTriple.δ gives a sequence \[\cdots \to H_n(B, A) \to H_n(D, A) \to H_n(D, B) \xrightarrow{\partial} H_{n-1}(B, A) \to \cdots \to H_0(D, A) \to H_0(D, B) \to 0\] exact everywhere Homology/TripleTopTriple.exact₁ Homology/TripleTopTriple.exact₂ Homology/TripleTopTriple.exact₃ Homology/TripleTopTriple.epi_map₂_zero.

Idea. The third isomorphism theorem \((C(D)/C(A))/(C(B)/C(A)) \cong C(D)/C(B)\), in any abelian category Homology/Triplecokernel_comp_shortExact.

Fact (excision) [V3.28] (standard). If \(Z \subseteq A \subseteq X\) and the closure of \(Z\) in \(X\) lies in the interior of \(A\) in \(X\), then \((X \setminus Z, A \setminus Z) \to (X, A)\) induces isomorphisms in all degrees. Homology/Excisionexcision

Idea. Hatcher’s proof (Prop. 2.21, Thm. 2.20): on a concrete model of singular chains, isomorphic to Mathlib’s Homology/SimplexsingChainsIso, barycentric subdivision with the diameter bound \((n/(n+1))^m\) shows that chains small for the cover \(\{A, X \setminus Z\}\) compute the homology, also modulo the chains of \(A\) Homology/SmallChainsquasiIso_smallQuotMap. In place of Hatcher’s order of a simplex, which faces need not respect, a Lebesgue-number order is used.

Fact (excision for an attached cell) [V3.31] (standard). Let \(E\) be Hausdorff, \(Y \subseteq X \subseteq E\) with \(Y\) closed in \(X\), \(V\) a finite-dimensional normed space with unit ball \(D\) and sphere \(S\), and \(\chi : V \to E\) continuous and injective on \(D\), with \(\chi(z) \in Y\) iff \(\|z\| = 1\) for \(z \in D\), and \(X = Y \cup \chi(D)\). Then \((\chi(D), \chi(S)) \to (X, Y)\) induces isomorphisms in all degrees. Homology/CellExcisioncellPair Homology/CellExcisionisIso_relHomology_map_cellPair

Idea. Milnor’s “by excision” (p. 29) is not literally one: the closure of \(Y \setminus \chi(S)\) meets \(\chi(S)\), which is not interior to \(Y\). With \(p = \chi(0)\), \(Y\) is a strong deformation retract of \(X \setminus \{p\}\), pushing the punctured cell radially onto \(\chi(S)\) Homology/CellExcisionisStrongDeformationRetract_sdiff_center; excise \(X \setminus \chi(D)\) from \((X, X \setminus \{p\})\), and compare with the cell alone.

Fact (cells) [V3.30] (standard). If \(E\) is Hausdorff and \(\chi : \mathbb R^k \to E\) is continuous and injective on \(D^k\), then \(H_k(\chi(D^k), \chi(S^{k-1})) \cong R\) and \(H_i(\chi(D^k), \chi(S^{k-1})) = 0\) for \(i \ne k\) Homology/SpherescellPairIso Homology/SpheresisZero_relHomology_cellPair. So does Mathlib’s disk pair \((\mathbb D^k, \partial\mathbb D^k)\) Homology/SpheresrelHomologyTopDiskPairIso.

Idea. Induction on \(k\): the cell contracts onto a point \(q \in \chi(S^k)\), so the boundary of the triple \(\{q\} \subseteq \chi(S^k) \subseteq \chi(D^{k+1})\) is an isomorphism; and the upper hemisphere is a \(k\)-cell attached to the lower one, which contracts onto \(q\).

Fact (attaching cells) [V3.31] (standard). In the setting of excision for an attached cell, with \(V = \mathbb R^k\) and \(Y\) closed in \(E\), the characteristic map \((\mathbb D^k, \partial\mathbb D^k) \to (X, Y)\) induces isomorphisms Homology/CellAttachrelHomology_cellAttach_iso: \(H_k(X, Y) \cong R\) and \(H_i(X, Y) = 0\) for \(i \ne k\) Homology/CellAttachrelHomologyCellAttachTopIso Homology/CellAttachisZero_relHomology_cellAttach. If \(\chi_j : \mathbb R^{k_j} \to E\), \(j \in s\) finite, are such maps with pairwise disjoint cells \(e_j = \chi_j(D^{k_j})\) and \(X = Y \cup \bigcup_j e_j\), then over a field \(\dim H_i(X, Y) = \#\{j : k_j = i\}\). Homology/CellAttachfinrank_relHomology_cellsAttach

Idea. One cell: the two previous facts. Several: attach them one at a time. Disjointness puts \(e_a\) inside the interior of \(Y \cup e_a\) in \(X_{s \cup a} = X_s \cup e_a\); excising \(e_a \setminus Y\) splits the sequence of the triple \(Y \subseteq X_s \subseteq X_{s \cup a}\) Homology/CellAttachTopTriple.isoBiprodOfRetraction, and dimensions add.

4.3 Singular homology of a filtration

From now on the coefficients are a field \(\mathbb k\).

Theorem (the Morse inequalities for a filtration of a space) [V3.32]. The sequence of a triple is a long exact sequence in the sense of §4.1 Homology/TripleFiltrationTopTriple.longExactSeq. Let \(X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots\) be subsets of a space and \(n \ge 1\), the steps \((X_{k+1}, X_k)\), \(k < n\), having finite-dimensional homology. Let \(b_i = \dim H_i(X_n, X_0)\) and \(C_i = \sum_{k < n} \dim H_i(X_{k+1}, X_k)\) Homology/TripleFiltrationsingularMorseNumber. Then:

  1. \(b_l \le C_l\) Homology/TripleFiltrationsingular_weak_morse_inequality;
  2. \(\sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i b_i = \sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i C_i\) if no step has homology in degree \(N + 1\) Homology/TripleFiltrationsingular_euler_characteristic;
  3. under the cell hypothesis of §4.1, \(C_i = \#\{p : \operatorname{ind} p = i\}\) Homology/TripleFiltrationsingularMorseNumber_eq_card, and \(b_\lambda \le \#\{p : \operatorname{ind} p = \lambda\}\) Homology/TripleFiltrationsingular_weak_morse_inequality_of_cells.

Proof. \(H(i, a, b) = H_i(X_{\max(a,b)}, X_a)\) Homology/TripleFiltrationsubsetHomology Homology/TripleFiltrationfiltrationGroup, with the sequences of triples and \(H_i(X_k, X_k) = 0\), is a homology of a filtration ([V3.9, §4.1], \(\iota = \mathbb N\)) as soon as all steps have finite-dimensional homology Homology/TripleFiltrationfiltrationHomology. Apply this to \(k \mapsto X_{\min(k, n)}\) Homology/TripleFiltrationtruncatedFiltrationHomology, whose later steps \((X_n, X_n)\) have zero homology and whose \(b_i\), \(C_i\) are those of \(X\); then [V3.11, §4.1]. \(\square\)

Definition (Betti numbers) [V3.33]. \(b_i(T) = \dim_{\mathbb k} H_i(T; \mathbb k)\), Mathlib’s singular homology, set to \(0\) if infinite-dimensional Homology/MorseHomologyBasicspaceHomology Homology/MorseHomologyBasicbettiNumber; it is \(\dim H_i(T, \emptyset)\) Homology/MorseHomologyBasicfinrank_subsetHomology_eq_bettiNumber.

Lemma (moving the bottom) [V3.33]. If \(A \subseteq B \subseteq D\) and \(A\) is a strong deformation retract of \(B\), then \(H_i(D, A) \cong H_i(D, B)\). Homology/MorseHomologyBasicsubsetHomologyEquivOfIsSDRBottom

Proof. In the sequence of the triple \(A \subseteq B \subseteq D\) every \(H_i(B, A)\) vanishes (§4.2), so each \(H_i(D, A) \to H_i(D, B)\) is injective by exactness and onto because \(\partial\) lands in \(0\) (in degree \(0\), by the end of the sequence) Homology/MorseHomologyBasicLongExactSeq.bijective_g_of_subsingleton. \(\square\)

Lemma (the slab, abstractly) [V3.33]. Let \(A \subseteq B \subseteq X' \subseteq X\) be subsets of a Hausdorff space \(E\), \(B\) closed, and \(\chi_j : \mathbb R^{k_j} \to E\), \(j < m\), continuous and injective on the unit balls, with pairwise disjoint cells \(e_j\) meeting \(B\) exactly in \(\chi_j(S^{k_j - 1})\) and \(B \cup \bigcup_j e_j \subseteq X'\). If \(A\) is a strong deformation retract of \(B\), \(B \cup \bigcup_j e_j\) one of \(X'\), and \(X'\) one of \(X\), then \(H_i(X, A)\) is finite-dimensional, of dimension \(\#\{j : k_j = i\}\). Homology/MorseHomologyBasicfinrank_subsetHomology_of_cells

Proof. \(H_i(X, A) \cong H_i(X, B) \cong H_i(X', B) \cong H_i(B \cup \bigcup_j e_j, B)\), moving the bottom, then the top twice (§4.2); the last is given by attaching cells, which holds over every field Homology/MorseHomologyBasicCellAttachHomology Homology/MorseHomologyCellscellAttachHomology. \(\square\)

4.4 The Morse filtration and Theorem 5.2

Let \(N \subseteq V\) be a compact slice submanifold modelled on \(Z\), \(F : V \to \mathbb R\) smooth, \(f = F|_N\) with every critical point non-degenerate, and \(N^a = \{f \le a\}\) [V2.1, §2.1]. There are finitely many critical points [V1.11, §1.7].

Definition [V3.16]. \(C_\lambda\) is the number of critical points of \(f\) of index \(\lambda\) (\(0\) if there are infinitely many). Chapter3/EulerCharcritCount

Homology is read in a space \(T\) in the universe of \(\mathbb k\) (§4.2) with a homeomorphism \(e : T \to N\), for instance \(N\) itself; strong deformation retracts carry over Chapter4/WhitneyIsStrongDeformationRetract.preimage_homeomorph.

Theorem (the homology of a slab) [V3.34]. Let \(a' \le a\) be values taken by no critical point, such that all critical values in \((a', a)\) are equal. Then \(H_i(N^a, N^{a'}; \mathbb k)\), read in \(T\), is finite-dimensional, of dimension the number of critical points of index \(i\) in \(f^{-1}(a', a)\). Homology/MorseHomologysublevel_step

Proof. If \((a', a)\) contains no critical value, \(N^{a'}\) is a strong deformation retract of \(N^a\) by Theorem 3.1 [V2.3, §2.3], and the group is \(0\). Otherwise let \(c\) be that value, \(S\) the critical points on \(f^{-1}(c)\), and \(\varepsilon_0 = \min(c - a', a - c)\). The compact \(f^{-1}[c - \varepsilon_0, c + \varepsilon_0]\) has no critical points outside \(S\), so Remark 3.3 [V2.9, §2.6] gives, for small \(\varepsilon < \varepsilon_0\), pairwise disjoint cells \(e_p\), \(p \in S\), of dimension the index of \(p\), meeting \(N^{c-\varepsilon}\) exactly in their boundary spheres, with \(N^{c-\varepsilon} \cup \bigcup_p e_p\) a strong deformation retract of \(N^{c+\varepsilon}\). Theorem 3.1 on \([a', c - \varepsilon]\) and \([c + \varepsilon, a]\) makes \(N^{a'}\) one of \(N^{c - \varepsilon}\) and \(N^{c+\varepsilon}\) one of \(N^a\). The slab lemma, with \((A, B, X', X) = (N^{a'}, N^{c-\varepsilon}, N^{c+\varepsilon}, N^a)\) carried to \(T\), concludes Homology/MorseHomologysublevel_step_critical. \(\square\)

Hidden hypothesis. Milnor’s \(H_*(M^{a_i}, M^{a_{i-1}}) = H_*(M^{a_{i-1}} \cup e, M^{a_{i-1}})\) is about pairs: the top must move along deformations fixing the bottom (strong deformation retracts, not homotopy types), and the bottom moves only in homology.

Theorem (the Morse filtration) [V3.34]. There are \(n \ge 1\) and values \(a_0 \le a_1 \le \cdots\) taken by no critical point, with \(N^{a_0} = \emptyset\), \(N^{a_n} = N\) and at most one critical value in each \((a_k, a_{k+1})\) Homology/MorseHomologyexists_morse_filtration. Hence \(X_k = e^{-1}(N^{a_k})\), with \(P\) the critical points, \(\operatorname{ind}\) the index and \(\operatorname{step}(p)\) the \(k < n\) with \(a_k < f(p) < a_{k+1}\), has finite-dimensional steps satisfying the cell hypothesis, \(X_0 = \emptyset\) and \(X_n = T\) Homology/MorseHomologyexists_cells_filtration; and \(C_\lambda = \#\{p : \operatorname{ind} p = \lambda\}\) Homology/MorseHomologycritCount_eq_card.

Proof. For a finite \(s \subseteq (L, \infty)\) there are \(n > 0\) and a monotone \(a\) with \(L < a_0\), no \(a_k\) in \(s\), \(s \subseteq (a_0, a_n)\) and at most one element of \(s\) in each \((a_k, a_{k+1})\), \(k < n\): induction on \(s\), prepending \((L + m)/2\) for a new minimum \(m\) Homology/MorseHomologyBasicexists_separating_seq. Apply it to the critical values. The minimum and the maximum of \(f\) are critical values Chapter2/CWTypeisCriticalPointM_of_forall_le Homology/MorseHomologyBasicisCriticalPointM_of_forall_ge, hence in \((a_0, a_n)\): \(N^{a_0} = \emptyset\), \(N^{a_n} = N\). Each step is a slab. The step of \(p\) exists because \(a_0 < f(p) < a_n\), and is unique because the intervals are disjoint. \(\square\)

Theorem 5.2 [V3.35]. Let \(N \subseteq V\) be a compact slice submanifold modelled on \(Z\), \(F : V \to \mathbb R\) smooth such that every critical point of \(f = F|_N\) is non-degenerate, \(\mathbb k\) a field, \(T\) a space in the universe of \(\mathbb k\) homeomorphic to \(N\) (for instance \(N\)), \(b_i = \dim_{\mathbb k} H_i(T; \mathbb k)\), and \(C_\lambda\) the number of critical points of \(f\) of index \(\lambda\). Then

  1. \(b_\lambda \le C_\lambda\) for every \(\lambda\) Homology/MorseHomologybettiNumber_le_critCount;
  2. \(\sum_{i=0}^{\dim Z} (-1)^i b_i = \sum_{\lambda=0}^{\dim Z} (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda\) Homology/MorseHomologysum_bettiNumber_eq_sum_critCount.

Proof. Take the filtration of the previous theorem: \(H_i(X_n, X_0) = H_i(T)\), and the cell hypothesis holds. (1) is [V3.32, §4.3] (3). For (2), no step has homology in degree \(\dim Z + 1\): by the cell hypothesis its dimension counts critical points of index \(\dim Z + 1\), and every index is at most \(\dim Z\) Chapter1/ManifoldindexM_le_finrank. Then [V3.32, §4.3] (2) and (3). \(\square\)
